t: Depth of BST Given Insertion Order — Depth From Predecessor and Successor
o: Insert the permutation order[0..n-1] into a BST — order[0] is the root and each later key lands in its unique BST position — then report the tree depth counted in NODES. Example 1, order = [2,1,4,3]: 2 is root, 1 goes left, 4 goes right, 3 becomes 4's left child, so depth 3. Example 3, [1,2,3,4]: a straight right spine gives depth 4. The catch is efficiency: n up to 10^5 with adversarial orders creates degenerate trees, so literal insertion walking from the root is O(n^2) in the worst case (a sorted order makes every walk linear), while the intended solution runs in O(n log n) without materializing the tree at all.
k: When a new key v is inserted, its parent is exactly its predecessor or successor among already-inserted keys — those two neighbors bracket v's empty slot in the tree.
Therefore depth(v) = 1 + max(depth(pred), depth(succ)) over whichever of the two exists; no child pointers are ever needed.
An ordered map (std::map / TreeMap / SortedList) returns pred and succ in O(log n), giving O(n log n) overall even for degenerate insertion orders.

a.i: Build the BST exactly as the statement describes: walk each key down from the root, branching by comparison until reaching an empty child slot; the number of edges walked is that node's depth minus one. Faithful to the process and easy to defend, but a sorted insertion order degenerates to a linked list and the total walking cost becomes quadratic.
s: Create the root from order[0] at depth 1.
For each subsequent value v, descend from the root comparing v with the current node.
Follow an existing left/right child when present; when the slot is empty, attach v there.
Track the depth incremented per edge traversed and update the global maximum with the landing depth.
Return the maximum after all insertions.
a.t: O(n x h) — h is the final tree height, O(n) for degenerate (e.g., sorted) orders.
a.sp: O(n) — child maps holding one entry per node.

a.n: Approach 2: Ordered Map Over Inserted Keys (Optimal)
a.i: Never build the tree. Maintain an ordered set of inserted keys with their depths. For a new key v, find pred = greatest inserted key below v and succ = smallest inserted key above v; these two bracket v's empty slot in the BST, so its parent is one of them and in all cases depth(v) = 1 + max(depth(pred), depth(succ)) ignoring missing sides. Record v's depth and keep the running maximum.
s: Initialize an empty ordered structure mapping key to depth.
For each v: locate pred (largest key < v) and succ (smallest key > v).
Set d = 1 + max(depth[pred] if any, depth[succ] if any).
Store depth[v] = d, insert v, update the answer maximum.
Return the maximum after processing the whole order.
a.t: O(n log n) — per insertion, O(log n) for the neighbor lookup and insert (JavaScript's binary-search-plus-splice variant shifts memory on insert but stays fast in practice).
a.sp: O(n) — depth table plus the ordered key collection.

w: The predecessor/successor identity is the star insight — justify it briefly: any previously inserted key whose search path could reach v's slot must be adjacent to v in sorted order, so one of them is the parent and their deeper side determines v's depth. Pitfalls: counting EDGES instead of NODES for the depth definition (a lone root has depth 1), mishandling a missing pred or succ at the extremes, and assuming any balancing happens — plain BSTs do not rotate. Edge cases: n = 1 (depth 1) and fully sorted orders (depth n). Follow-up: report depths online while insertions stream (this solution already does), or support deletions via the same ordered map.
